title: Searing
summary: Browning the surface of meat or fish in a very hot pan for flavour (the Maillard reaction). It does not 'seal in juices' — it makes taste.
body:
Take the meat out of the fridge 20–30 min before and pat it completely dry with kitchen paper.
Salt it generously just before cooking.
Heat a heavy pan (stainless or cast iron) on high until a drop of water dances and evaporates instantly, then add a thin film of sunflower oil.
Lay the meat in AWAY from you and do not touch it for 2–3 minutes.
It releases from the pan by itself when a brown crust has formed — then turn it.
tips:
A wet surface steams instead of browning — dry it.
An overcrowded pan drops in temperature; cook in batches.
Non-stick pans do not build fond (the brown bits for a pan sauce).
img: a thick steak searing in a hot stainless steel pan, golden brown crust, wisps of smoke

title: Sautéing & sweating onions
summary: Cooking chopped vegetables in a little fat over medium heat, stirring — soft and sweet (sweat) or golden (sauté).
body:
Heat the pan on medium, add oil or butter.
Add the onion with a pinch of salt (salt draws out water so it softens without browning).
Stir every minute or so.
Sweat = 6–10 min until soft and see-through, no colour.
Sauté/brown = 12–15 min until golden.
tips:
Add garlic only in the last minute — it burns in seconds and turns bitter.
If onions catch, add a splash of water and turn the heat down.
img: diced onions softening in olive oil in a pan, translucent, wooden spoon

title: Deglazing
summary: Pouring liquid into a hot pan to lift the brown bits (fond) stuck to the bottom — the flavour base of every pan sauce.
body:
After searing, take the meat out and pour off most of the fat.
With the pan still hot, pour in stock (or vinegar, or water) — it will hiss.
Scrape the bottom with a wooden spoon until all the brown bits dissolve.
Now reduce it.
tips:
Black bits are burnt, not fond — if the pan is black, wipe it and start the sauce fresh.
No wine needed: stock plus a splash of red wine vinegar gives the acidity.
img: stock being poured into a hot pan with browned bits, steam rising, wooden spoon scraping

title: Reducing
summary: Boiling a liquid to evaporate water so the flavour concentrates and it thickens.
body:
Bring the liquid to a lively simmer in a wide pan (more surface = faster).
Watch it: it is ready when it coats the back of a spoon and a finger drawn through leaves a clear line.
Taste only AFTER reducing — salt concentrates too.
tips:
Season at the end; a reduced stock-cube sauce can become far too salty.
A wide sauté pan reduces in half the time of a deep saucepan.
img: sauce reducing in a wide pan, glossy bubbles, spoon coated with sauce

title: Making a roux
summary: Equal weights of butter and flour cooked together — it thickens milk (béchamel) or stock (velouté, gravy).
body:
Melt the butter on medium heat.
Add the same weight of flour and stir to a paste.
Cook it, stirring, 2 minutes for a white roux (no colour), longer for blond or brown.
Add the liquid a little at a time, whisking hard after each addition until smooth.
Simmer at least 5 minutes to cook out the floury taste.
tips:
Cold liquid into hot roux (or hot into cold) avoids lumps.
Lumpy? Whisk hard or blitz with a stick blender.
Too thick: whisk in more liquid. Too thin: simmer longer.
img: butter and flour paste bubbling in a saucepan with a whisk, pale golden roux

title: Emulsifying
summary: Forcing fat and water to mix into a smooth sauce — hollandaise, aioli, beurre blanc, vinaigrette.
body:
Start with the water-based part (yolks, reduction, vinegar, mustard).
Add the fat SLOWLY — drops at first, then a thin stream — whisking all the time.
Keep warm sauces warm, not hot: hollandaise splits above ~65 °C, beurre blanc if it boils.
tips:
Split sauce? Whisk a fresh yolk (or a spoon of hot water) in a clean bowl and slowly whisk the split sauce into it.
Mustard and egg yolk are natural emulsifiers.
img: whisking a glossy yellow hollandaise in a bowl over a pan of simmering water

title: Thickening with a starch slurry
summary: Corn flour mixed with cold water and stirred into a simmering liquid — thick and glossy in one minute.
body:
Mix 1 tsp corn flour with 1 tbsp COLD water until smooth.
Bring the sauce to a simmer.
Stir the slurry in and keep stirring.
It thickens as soon as it bubbles again; simmer 30–60 seconds.
Add more slurry only if needed — 1 tsp thickens about 250 ml lightly.
tips:
Never add dry starch to hot liquid — instant lumps.
Over-boiling for a long time can thin it again.
Glossy, gluten-free and lighter than a roux.
img: pouring a white corn starch slurry from a small glass into a simmering pan of sauce

title: Using & making stock
summary: Stock is flavoured water: the liquid base of sauces, soups, risotto and gravy. Homemade is better and nearly free; cubes are the fallback.
body:
Chicken: roast-chicken carcass + 1 onion + 1 carrot + 1 celery stick + bay leaf + peppercorns, cover with cold water.
Bring slowly to a simmer, skim the grey foam, never boil hard (it goes cloudy).
Simmer 2–3 h (or slow cooker LOW 8–10 h).
Strain, cool quickly (sink of cold water), refrigerate; lift off the fat.
Freeze in 500 ml tubs and ice-cube trays.
tips:
Vegetable stock: onion, carrot, celery, mushrooms, parsley stalks, 45 min.
Cubes: use half a cube more water than the pack says and salt at the end — they are salty.
Fridge 3–4 days, freezer 2–3 months.
img: a large pot of golden chicken stock with vegetables and herbs simmering on a stove

title: Resting meat
summary: Letting cooked meat sit before cutting so the juices settle instead of running onto the board.
body:
Move the meat to a warm plate or board.
Cover loosely with foil (tight foil steams the crust).
Rest steaks 5 min, chicken 10–15 min, big roasts 20–30 min.
The inside keeps cooking 2–5 °C — take it off a little early.
tips:
Pour the resting juices into the sauce.
Slice against the grain (across the lines of the muscle).
img: a cooked steak resting on a wooden board loosely covered with foil

title: Knife cuts & the claw grip
summary: Hold the knife by the blade (pinch grip), curl the guiding hand's fingertips under (the claw), and keep the tip on the board.
body:
Pinch the blade just in front of the handle between thumb and index finger; other fingers round the handle.
Guiding hand: fingertips tucked in, knuckles against the flat of the blade.
Rock the knife: tip stays on the board, heel goes up and down.
Onion dice: halve through the root, peel, make horizontal then vertical cuts not through the root, then slice across.
Mince garlic: crush with the flat of the knife, chop, rock over it with a pinch of salt.
tips:
A sharp knife is safer than a blunt one — it does not slip.
Put a damp cloth under the board so it does not move.
Keep fingers curled; the knuckles guide.
img: hands dicing an onion on a wooden board with a chef's knife using the claw grip

title: Garlic: peel, slice, mince, paste
summary: One press with the flat of the knife takes the skin off. Then slice it for mild, mince it for strong, mash it for raw sauces.
body:
Peel: lay the clove on the board, put the flat of a big knife on it and press once with the heel of your hand. The skin splits and slides off.
Cut off the hard root end.
Sliced (pan sauces, roasting with tomatoes): thin slices across the clove. Mild, slow to burn.
Minced (marinades, quick sauces): slice lengthwise, turn, slice across, then rock the knife over the pile a few times. Stronger.
Paste (dressings, raw sauces): mince, add a pinch of salt and drag the flat of the blade across it until smooth.
In the pan: add it to the oil about 30 seconds before the next ingredient. Pale gold is done.
tips:
Brown garlic is bitter: if it went dark, wipe the pan and start again, it takes a minute.
The finer you cut it, the stronger it tastes and the faster it burns.
Soft enough to mash into a sauce: whole peeled cloves in a dish with oil, air fryer 190 °C for 20 minutes. In a pan they stay hard, so slice them.
One clove is about 5 g. A green shoot in the middle tastes sharp: pull it out for raw sauces.
Smell on your fingers: rub them on the steel of the tap under cold water.
img: hands slicing peeled garlic cloves thinly on a wooden board with a chef's knife, whole garlic bulb beside

title: Seasoning & tasting
summary: Taste at every stage; balance salt, acid, fat and heat.
body:
Season meat before cooking, sauces at the end.
Taste: flat → salt. Heavy or dull → acid (lemon, vinegar). Too sharp → a little fat (butter, oil). Too salty → acid and more unsalted liquid.
Use a clean spoon each time.
tips:
Season from a height so the salt spreads evenly.
Pasta water should taste like the sea (about 10 g salt per litre).
img: a hand sprinkling salt from a height over a pan of vegetables

title: Doneness & a thermometer
summary: An instant-read thermometer ends guessing. Check the thickest part, away from bone.
body:
Chicken & turkey: 74 °C (the safe temperature).
Pork: 63 °C plus rest (blush pink is fine), pulled pork 90–95 °C.
Beef steak: rare 50–52, medium-rare 54–57, medium 60–63 °C (whole muscle; mince 71 °C).
Lamb: medium 60–63 °C; slow-cooked lamb shoulder until it falls apart.
Fish: 60–63 °C or flakes easily and is opaque.
Reheated leftovers: piping hot right through (75 °C).
tips:
Take meat off 2–3 °C before the target — it rises while resting.
Wash the probe between raw and cooked checks.
img: an instant-read digital meat thermometer inserted into a roast chicken thigh

title: Using a slow cooker
summary: Low steady heat for hours — perfect for tough cuts, stock and meal-prep batches.
body:
Brown meat first in a pan for flavour (optional but better).
Put root veg at the bottom, meat on top; liquid only about halfway — the lid traps moisture.
LOW 7–9 h or HIGH 4–5 h for stews.
Do not lift the lid — each peek adds ~20 minutes.
Thicken at the end with a corn-flour slurry if needed.
tips:
Never put frozen meat in — it stays in the danger zone too long. Thaw first.
Fill between half and two-thirds.
Add delicate things (herbs, yogurt, peas) in the last 30 min.
img: a slow cooker with lid off showing a rich stew with chunks of meat and vegetables

title: Using a blender
summary: For smooth sauces, soups and smoothies. Liquids first, then soft, then hard.
body:
Put liquids in first, then soft ingredients, then hard ones and ice on top.
Start on low, then increase.
Hot soup: fill only half, remove the centre cap and cover with a folded towel so steam escapes.
Pulse for chunky sauces (chimichurri), run for smooth (romesco).
tips:
Pesto keeps its colour if you blitz quickly — long blending heats and darkens the basil.
A stick blender works for sauces in the pan.
img: a blender jug filled with green herbs, garlic and olive oil, about to be blended

title: Using an air fryer
summary: A small fan oven: fast, crisp, little oil.
body:
Preheat 3 minutes.
Lightly oil or spray the food, not the basket.
One layer, gaps between pieces — never overcrowd.
Shake or turn halfway.
Rough guide: chicken thighs 200 °C 18–22 min (to 74 °C), salmon skin-side up 200 °C 8–10 min, halloumi 200 °C 6–8 min, broccoli/cauliflower 190 °C 10–12 min.
tips:
Check a minute or two early the first time — models differ.
Paper liners help with sticky marinades.
Meat still needs the thermometer.
img: golden crispy chicken thighs in an open air fryer basket

title: Freezing, thawing & cooling food safely
summary: Cool cooked food fast, freeze in flat labelled portions, thaw in the fridge.
body:
Cool cooked food quickly: spread it out in a shallow container, or stand the pot in a sink of cold water; into the fridge within 2 hours (rice within 1 hour).
Portion into containers or flat freezer bags, squeeze out air.
Label: what, date, portions.
Thaw in the fridge (overnight), or in cold water in a sealed bag, or in the microwave and cook straight away.
Reheat until steaming hot all the way through; reheat only once.
tips:
Never refreeze raw meat that was thawed — cook it first, then you may freeze the cooked dish.
Freezer at −18 °C; fridge at 5 °C or below.
Cooked leftovers: fridge 3–4 days, freezer 2–3 months for best quality.
img: labelled flat freezer bags and glass meal-prep containers being stacked in a freezer
